title: Fergus Baker wins Vice-Chancellor’s Prize for Best Doctoral Thesis
text:
Congratulations to Dr Fergus Baker on receiving the University of Bristol’s Vice-Chancellor’s Prize for Best Doctoral Thesis.



Dr Fergus Baker


Fergus’s thesis, General relativistic effects in black hole X-ray coronal models, was supervised by me and Dr Sotiria Fotopoulou. His examiners highlighted the novel physical insights, mathematical and computational techniques, and the software package he released for the community.
You can read his thesis here: General relativistic effects in black hole X-ray coronal models. The source code is also there so you can see how the figures were made. The thesis is a work of art and an excellent introduction to the field. Well done Fergus, we’re very proud of you!
Fergus is now a postdoctoral researcher at Durham.

title: About
text: I am a Professor in the School of Physics at the University of Bristol. I completed my PhD at Cambridge with Andy Fabian on X-ray studies of accreting black holes, then held Chandra postdoctoral positions at the University of Maryland (with Andrew Wilson) and MIT (with Claude Canizares). I joined Bristol in 2007.

title: About
text:
Research
My research interests include numerical and observational astrophysics focused on accreting black holes. The numerical work involves the development of general relativistic models of the time-dependent spectra of accretion flows with different disc, corona, and spacetime geometries. The observational work concerns the analysis of X-ray data from accreting black holes using telescopes such as XMM-Newton, Chandra, and NuSTAR.
Notes on relativistic accretion discs and related software are collected in the project wiki.

title: Quarto lecture notes
text:
Several people have asked how I prepare lecture notes in HTML and PDF. Here’s an overview of the workflow. This is slightly different from how I do it day to day because I use a “book” project rather than a “website” project, but the principles are the same.
Here’s an example site.

title: Quarto lecture notes
section: Set up an empty GitHub repository
text:
Set up an empty GitHub repository
Start with a blank repository containing a README.md and a LICENSE. I’ve used the MIT license. Alternatively, create the Quarto project first and push everything afterwards.
The example repository is andys-quarto-example.

title: Quarto lecture notes
text:
Install Quarto
Follow the Quarto get-started instructions. On a Mac with Homebrew: brew install --cask quarto.

title: Quarto lecture notes
text:
Editor setup
Install the Quarto VS Code / Cursor extension.

title: Quarto lecture notes
text:
Start a Quarto website project
You can use “Quarto: Create New Project” and choose “Website Project”, or add a few files by hand:

_quarto.yml — project configuration
index.md — home page
about.md — another page
styles.css — optional styling

See the files in the example repository.

title: Quarto lecture notes
text:
Publishing
Follow the Quarto GitHub Pages instructions. For a simple start you can render to docs/ and deploy from that folder; a GitHub Action is usually better for keeping the site up to date automatically.
Published example: https://phajy.github.io/andys-quarto-example/.

title: Quarto lecture notes
text:
Add content
Headings, figures, and mathematics follow standard Quarto Markdown. For example:
## Parallel-transport and geodesics

![Parallel transport of a vector.](parallel_transport.png){width=300 #fig-parallel-transport}

We can use parallel transport to construct *geodesics*:

$$
\begin{aligned}
    \pmb{\nabla}_{\vec u} {\vec u} &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$
More in the Quarto Markdown documentation.
